A.explanation: At $t = Z$ the velocity is constant because the graph is horizontal, so acceleration is $0$, not $g$.

B.explanation: At $t = Y$ the gradient is still positive but getting smaller, so acceleration is decreasing, and at $t = Z$ the gradient is zero, so acceleration is $0$.

C.explanation: The velocity-time graph is curved with falling gradient, not a straight line, so acceleration at $t = Y$ is not constant.

D.explanation: Zero acceleration at $t = Z$ is correct for terminal velocity, but acceleration at $t = Y$ is still changing as air resistance grows.

hints: Recall that on a velocity-time graph the acceleration is the gradient, $a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$.
Look at how the steepness changes up to $t = Y$ - the curve is still rising but flattening as air resistance increases with speed.
Look at the shape at $t = Z$ - the velocity stops increasing and the graph becomes horizontal, so work out what zero gradient means for acceleration.
walkthrough: Identify the rule: gradient of a velocity-time graph equals acceleration, so a steeper slope means larger acceleration and a horizontal section means zero acceleration.
At $t = Y$ the graph is still rising, so velocity is increasing and acceleration is positive, but the curve is bending over so its gradient is getting smaller with time.
This decreasing gradient is caused by air resistance increasing with speed, reducing the resultant downward force, so acceleration at $t = Y$ is described as decreasing.
At $t = Z$ the graph has levelled off to a horizontal line, so $\Delta v = 0$ over time and the gradient is zero, which is terminal velocity where drag balances weight.
Zero gradient means zero acceleration at $t = Z$. Combining decreasing at $t = Y$ with $0$ at $t = Z$. This is option B.
